_note: What MyThuso can actually do, and what it only draws. Every screen used to carry its own hand-typed 'Design preview', 'Demonstration record' or 'Fictional workspace' — sixty-odd sentences saying roughly the same thing in slightly different words, some of them on screens whose function was by then real, and none of them connected to anything that would know. This file is the one place that knows. A capability is connected or it is not; a screen asks, and the notice is rendered from here or not rendered at all. When an integration lands, one boolean changes and the sentence disappears from every platform at once.
_honestyNote: Turning `connected` to true is a claim about the world, not about the code, so scripts/check-boundaries.mjs refuses it unless `evidence` names a file that exists and the capability's `blockedBy` list is empty. A health service that overstates its readiness is not a marketing problem, and the way that happens is never a lie — it is somebody tidying a banner off a layout at eleven at night.

capabilities._whyNotSimulated: Marked simulated on 10 September and put back the same day, because nothing was ever built to stand behind it. The simulation notice said 'the controls around them are real and are exercised against this data', and no simulator was exercising anything — a false sentence on a clinical screen, which is the exact failure the third state was introduced to prevent rather than to commit. It is the one capability whose seam is a refusal by design: feeds.json's noSeam entry says there is no ingestion route for a clinical record and there must not be one. A record store standing in here is buildable and worth building — it would exercise the consent gate, the access log and the export against fictional people — but it is a piece of work, not a state change, and the state may not run ahead of it.

capabilities.name: Talking to GilbertOne
blockedBy: No contracted South African speech provider: so English only, and only on phones that recognise it offline.

No contracted language model. Where GilbertOne's approved sentences cannot place a message, it may be sent to Azure OpenAI, running in South Africa, after details that could identify somebody are removed. That has been live since 21 September 2026 without a signed DPIA, an Information Officer or a residency decision (docs/governance/ASSISTANT-ACTIVATION.md). Emergencies and refusals are always answered by the approved sentences.
No decision about a recording beyond keeping none, so nothing is recorded on any platform, and on a phone no transcript leaves it.

On the web the microphone is real and the browser's own recognition does the work, which may carry what is said to the company that makes the browser. That route is disclosed before the first tap rather than removed, and no speech provider of MyThuso's is contracted to replace it.
No clinical or privacy review of patients speaking into a browser, so the web microphone is offered on the founder's decision of 18 September 2026 and not on a reviewer's.
capabilities.notice: GilbertOne listens only after you tap, hears English only, and keeps no recording. On a phone the words are turned into text on the phone itself. On the web — in the assistant, and on the labelled GilbertOne demonstrator — the browser's own recognition does the work, and it may send what you say to the company that makes the browser; MyThuso is not that company and keeps nothing. Either way the words are shown to you to check before you send them, and typing always works. When GilbertOne's approved sentences cannot answer what you sent, it may be sent to the language model MyThuso uses, after details that could identify you have been removed, so please avoid typing identifying health information. Emergencies are always answered by the approved sentences.
capabilities.neverSoften: No listening affordance may be drawn unless the microphone is actually open — not an enabled one, not a disabled one, not a decorative one. On the web a microphone may open in the live assistant and on the labelled GilbertOne demonstrator, nowhere else, only after an explicit tap, and only with the disclosure about the browser's own recognition shown before the first one; every other web surface offers nothing in any state. A control that looks like it is listening and is not is worse than no control, and on a health product it is the kind of worse that gets believed.

onDevice.what: English push-to-talk recognised by the phone's own recogniser with no network: on iOS with requiresOnDeviceRecognition, on Android 12 and later with the on-device recogniser.
onDevice.whyNotConnected: Nothing is contracted and nothing leaves the phone, so the notice stays.

webPoc.what: Real push-to-talk and real speech on the GilbertOne character demonstrator, through the browser's own SpeechRecognition and SpeechSynthesis: the microphone opens on a tap, closes on Stop or at the listening cap, and the words it caught are shown to be corrected or discarded before they go anywhere. The demonstrator answers nothing — there is no model behind it and no request leaves the page.
webPoc.whyNotTheLiveProduct: What still separates the two is not the microphone but what answers. The demonstrator says nothing back, asks nothing of a patient, and is labelled a demonstrator on every screen of it; the live assistant answers from an approved set of sentences, asks a language model where they cannot place a message (since 21 September 2026), and carries a person's question wherever it leads. Both take the same browser route, because a browser's recognition may send what is said to the company that makes the browser, and MDN says so — so both disclose it before the first tap, on the founder's decision of 18 September 2026. Widening the route did not widen what the demonstrator is allowed to become.

rules.statement: A screen renders the notice for the capability it depends on. Not three of them stacked, and not one it does not use.
rules.why: A nurse's schedule carried a Design preview banner, a WORKSPACE · DEMO eyebrow and a Fictional workspace paragraph before any content — three sentences saying one thing, filling the screen above the first visit. A reader who is told the same thing three times has been told it none.

rules.statement: No screen writes its own not-connected sentence. It names a capability and the sentence is rendered from this file.
rules.why: Sixty hand-typed variations cannot be switched off together, and some of them will be wrong. One place that knows means one boolean to change when an integration lands.

rules.statement: A capability may be marked connected only when `evidence` names a file that exists and `blockedBy` is empty. The build refuses it otherwise.
rules.why: The failure mode is never a lie. It is somebody clearing a banner off a layout because the screenshot looked better without it.

rules.statement: A state picker and a gallery of loading states are development tools. They are removed from what ships, and removing them says nothing about whether anything is connected.
rules.why: The two got tangled: taking the demo furniture out felt like claiming the product was live. They are separate questions and this file answers only the second. This rule named a role switcher as well until 12 September, when the founder made one the way in; see a-demo-login-is-not-an-account for why that is a change to what ships rather than to what is claimed.

rules.statement: The demo login is what ships, because there is nothing to sign in to. Every surface it opens renders the accounts notice, and the switcher says in the contract's own words that it grants no role.
rules.why: Four sign-in screens each carried this capability's notice, each explained that there are no accounts, and each then asked the reader to choose a workspace anyway. Replacing them with one switcher is honest about what was already happening — but it moves the notice off four screens at once, and a screen that stops speaking is exactly the disclosure failure a-simulation-says-so exists to refuse. So the notice moves with it rather than being dropped, and the switcher carries the refusal too: an auto login that looks like an account is worse than a sign-in wall with nothing behind it, because the wall at least admits it is a door.

rules.statement: `state: simulated` never sets `connected: true`, and the two may not disagree. A simulated capability still lists everything blocking it.
rules.why: The whole hazard of a simulator is that it works. A person who has watched a payment go through end to end is one edit away from believing a payment provider exists, and the status page is the page a funder reads. So the boolean that removes every notice in the product is left alone, and the build fails if the state and the boolean drift apart.

rules.statement: A simulated capability renders its simulation notice, word for word, wherever the absent notice would have rendered. No screen may be quieter for being simulated than it was for being absent.
rules.why: The failure mode is not a screen that lies. It is a screen that stops speaking: the sentence goes away because something now answers, and nobody notices that what answers is a fixture. Silence is the disclosure failure, so the notice never disappears until the state is connected.

rules.statement: No simulator may be reached over HTTP. Every feed route goes on refusing every payload, and a simulated event enters in process through a function of its own.
rules.why: apps/api/src/feeds/index.ts argues that a route which could accept under some condition is a route somebody finds the condition for, usually late at night with a vendor on the phone. A simulation flag on those routes would be exactly that condition. So `decide` still has no acceptance to construct, and the simulators sit beside the boundary rather than inside it.

rules.statement: `voice` alone is on-device: the phone recognises speech, GilbertOne answers from a contract, and nothing is connected.
rules.why: English push-to-talk on the phone, decided on 14 September 2026, is neither a stand-in answering (simulated) nor a supplier (connected). The state says exactly what is true, and the notice stays.

flags.statement: The unified conversation surface is behind a flag: with it off, every platform answers from the contract with no network at all; with it on, a native build may ask POST /assistant/v1/turn after a message the local matcher could not place.
flags.why: The service is real and is not deployed: it answers on loopback, and a phone in somebody's hand cannot reach that. A boolean that is false by default is the difference between a build that quietly reaches for an address the day somebody else runs it and one that reaches for it the day this file says so. The web panel reads no flag — its requests go through its own origin's proxy, which is the path a deploy changes — so the flag is for the natives, whose releases outlive a deploy.

requiresPermissions.serves: Reaching the unified conversation surface at /assistant/v1/turn once the flag is on. Android needs this permission to open any connection; iOS reads no key for the same request, which is why this flag names one platform.

_permissionsNote: A permission may exist only when a capability or flag names it under requiresPermissions, with its platform and the feature it serves; scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails any other. Today there are four: three for GilbertOne's push-to-talk and one for the unified conversation flag. No camera, no location, nothing for the consultation.
_simulationNote: A capability has four states; `on-device` is voice's alone (see voice-is-on-device), and the other three are these. `absent` means nothing is behind it and the screen says so. `connected` means a contracted supplier answers, and the rule connected-needs-evidence holds it to a file that exists and an empty blockedBy. `simulated` is the third: a named simulator, running in this process, producing what the supplier would produce so the product can be walked end to end before anybody has signed anything. It was added because the founder asked to see the whole journey work, and the honest way to give him that is a third state rather than the second one. Marking these connected would have removed the notice from every screen and told a funder reading the status page that a health service is live. A simulated capability keeps its notice and changes what it says: not 'this is not switched on' but 'this is simulated, and here is what the simulation will not do'. blockedBy is untouched by simulation, because a simulator does not unblock anything — the SMS provider is still unsigned the day the simulated one works perfectly.
